opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that the models we have today aren't really learning after deployment. They're trained once, and then they're frozen. Everything that happens afterward, in-context learning, the KV cache, retrieval, is a kind of short-term memory. When the context window ends, it's gone. It's a bit like anterograde amnesia: you remember everything up to some point in the past, and you can hold the present in your head for a few minutes, but nothing new ever consolidates.

So for me, an ideal continually learning system should have a few properties.

First, memory shouldn't be a binary of "short-term attention" versus "long-term weights." The brain doesn't work that way. It has a spectrum of memory systems that update at different frequencies. Some things change every few milliseconds, some over hours, and some during sleep through consolidation. That's the intuition behind what we've been calling nested learning. You view the model as a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency. Attention is the fastest level, the slow pretrained weights are the slowest level, and an ideal system has a continuum in between, so information can gradually move from fast, transient memory into more persistent memory.

Second, the system should decide what is worth remembering. In Titans we used a notion of "surprise": the gradient of the memory's loss with respect to the input. If something violates your expectations, that's a signal you should store it. You also need momentum, because an event that's surprising makes what comes right after it important too, and you need forgetting, a decay or weight-decay-style gate. Without forgetting, memory saturates and you get interference. So learning, remembering, and forgetting are really one design problem, not three.

Third, it should learn at test time without catastrophic forgetting. That's the classic continual learning problem, and I think part of the answer is architectural. If you have multiple levels, new knowledge lands first in the faster, more plastic components, and only what proves useful over time gets consolidated into the slower ones. You're not overwriting your core knowledge every time you see something new.

Fourth, and this is more speculative, the ideal system should be somewhat self-modifying. It should learn not just the content but how to update itself, essentially learning its own learning rule. That's what we explored with HOPE, a self-referential module layered with a continuum memory system. The optimizer itself is a kind of associative memory, so in principle you can make that part learnable too.

Practically, what you'd see from the outside is a model you use for a week that actually gets better at your codebase or your research problem. It remembers what mattered, quietly lets go of what didn't, and doesn't need someone to retrain it from scratch or to stuff everything back into a giant prompt. We're not there yet, but I think the path is less about bigger context windows and more about giving models a real, multi-timescale memory that keeps learning.

r001.rationale: The response advocates learning at test time and mentions pretrained weights, but it does not assert that training and testing phases are absent or unified.

r002.rationale: It mentions sleep and different update frequencies, but does not distinguish active and sleep phases by whether external input is received.

r003.rationale: It mentions sleep-based consolidation, but does not say the model should use periods without external input to process learned information for self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, an ideal continually learning system should look a lot more like how humans actually learn than how we currently train models, which is basically: collect a giant static dataset, run one big training phase, freeze the weights, and then deploy. That's a strange setup if you think about it. The world keeps changing after the training cutoff, the user keeps giving the model new information, and the model just... can't absorb any of it into its parameters. Everything new has to live in the context window, and the context window is both expensive and forgetful in its own way.

So the first property I'd want is that learning never really stops. There shouldn't be a hard line between "training time" and "test time." When the model sees a new document, a new conversation, a new piece of feedback, it should be able to update some internal state in a way that actually persists, not just attend over it once and throw it away.

The second property, which is harder, is that this updating has to be selective. You don't want to memorize everything you see, because most of what you see isn't worth remembering. Humans are pretty good at this. Something surprising, something that violates your expectations, tends to stick. Something totally routine doesn't. So I think a good continual learner needs a notion of surprise or novelty that drives what gets written into memory, and some notion of forgetting so that memory doesn't just fill up with noise and drift.

Third, I think you need multiple timescales of memory working together. There's very short-term stuff, basically what's in your working context right now. There's medium-term stuff, things from this session or this week that you want to keep around and consolidate. And then there's long-term knowledge that's much more stable and only changes slowly. In current architectures those are kind of collapsed together: attention handles the short term, and the pretrained weights handle the long term, with nothing in between. A lot of what we've been working on is about filling in that middle layer, having a memory module that is itself a learnable component, that updates its own parameters at test time based on what it sees, but does so with its own learning rate and its own forgetting mechanism so it doesn't destabilize the rest of the model.

And then the fourth thing, which people underrate, is that the system should learn how to learn. It's not enough to have a memory that updates. The rules for when and how to update should themselves be shaped by training, so that by the time you deploy the model, it has a good inductive bias for what's worth keeping. Otherwise you end up hand-designing the memory heuristics, and those tend to break the moment the distribution shifts.

If you put all of that together, the ideal is something that behaves like a single model but is really a stack of learners operating at different speeds, each one deciding what to pass down to the slower one below it. That's roughly the mental picture I'm chasing. We're not there yet, but I think the pieces are starting to exist.

r001.rationale: The response says there should be “no hard line” between training time and test time, clearly asserting that continual learning has no separate phases.

r002.rationale: It discusses updating memory when new information arrives but does not distinguish active and sleep phases by whether external input is present.

r003.rationale: It mentions memory consolidation and forgetting, but does not propose using periods without external input to process prior learning for self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think an ideal continually learning AI should be able to learn from its experience without having to start over. As it encounters new information, it should decide what matters, how that relates to what it already knows, and whether it needs to revise an existing belief or learn something new.

That doesn’t mean changing all of its knowledge after every interaction. Some information is useful only in the current context; other information should become part of its long-term memory. So you want learning at different timescales—fast adaptation to what’s happening now, and slower changes that consolidate what remains useful across experiences.

The challenge is balancing adaptation with stability. A system that remembers everything indiscriminately will accumulate noise, and a system that constantly overwrites its knowledge will forget useful things. Ideally, it can keep learning while preserving the capabilities it has already developed, and recognize when it doesn’t yet have enough evidence to make a lasting change.

r001.rationale: The response describes ongoing learning without starting over, but does not say that training and testing phases are absent.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes fast adaptation from slower consolidation, not active and sleep phases based on whether external input is received.

r003.rationale: It mentions consolidating useful knowledge across experiences, but does not propose using periods without external input to process past learning for self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an ideal continually learning AI should be able to learn from its experience without having to start over every time it encounters something new. It should integrate new information into what it already knows, while preserving the knowledge and skills that are still useful.

But that doesn’t mean updating everything all the time. Some information is relevant only to the current conversation; other information should change the system’s understanding over the long term. So it needs a way to decide what to remember, what to consolidate, and what to forget—and those processes might operate at different timescales.

The goal is a system that can adapt while remaining stable. It should become more capable through interaction, without every new experience overwriting what it learned before.
